html:
SMTO-API-0006 — SMTO needs you to sign in again

GUID: d1ca7007-afac-4f01-9a07-ae75ddb8d9ad
Slug: api-authentication-required
Domain: API · Subsystem: api

What happened

  • SMTO didn't accept this request because it couldn't confirm who you are. Your sign-in may have ended, or another tab may be signed in with a different account.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. On the Sign in to your workspace page (SMTO usually opens it for you), enter your username and password and select Sign in. Signing in gives this browser a fresh session that SMTO recognizes.
  2. If you have SMTO open in several tabs, close the extra tabs or make sure they all use the same account, then reload this page. SMTO turns away requests from a page that was opened under a different account.
  3. After signing in, check whether the change you were making is already there before doing it again. SMTO doesn't repeat your action for you after sign-in, so you may need to do it once more.

What success looks like

  • SMTO opens without asking you to sign in again, and your action works.

If it still fails

  • If SMTO says your username or password is wrong, ask an administrator to reset your password. Never type your password into a task, a chat message or a screenshot. Send the details from Copy error details to the person who manages SMTO.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • An SMTO or Gateway endpoint returned HTTP 401 (no valid session, or the session's account differs from the one the page was opened with) and no more specific registered cause applied.

What this means

  • HTTP enrichment finds no more specific registered cause and maps status 401 to the API authentication category. Generic API status and exception families establish only their stated boundary. Stronger structured causes take precedence; the original receipt determines whether work started or had effects, and diagnostics add no dispatch or retry.

Why this can happen

  • HTTP enrichment finds no more specific registered cause and maps status 401 to the API authentication category.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the actual API route and supported login challenge; the status alone does not identify a particular expired credential.

How to fix it

  • Re-authenticate through the portal sign-in page (/login) for browser clients; for the CLI, pass --portal-username and --portal-password-file to aor run or aor doctor --server-url. If a signed-in browser keeps getting 401, check for an account_changed response from a tab opened under another account and for a missing or expired session cookie.
  • Authenticate through the supported client flow for this API.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • The intended client authenticates through the route's supported flow.

What not to do

  • Do not put credentials in task text, command arguments, screenshots or diagnostic reports.

Technical notes

  • Generic API status and exception families establish only their stated boundary. Stronger structured causes take precedence; the original receipt determines whether work started or had effects, and diagnostics add no dispatch or retry.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
